Thirty-four comments

The tune itself

Ok…when I play up in Fall River, Massachusetts, this is how I play the tune. First in D, then G, then A (obviously). I figured I’d spread the trend and put all three versions on here.

↳ Posted by Josh Kane on March 13th, 2002.

Playing in all those different keys isn’t an unusual way of playing this tune. In fact, I’ve never heard it played any other way *except* with all those key changes.

The only thing is; I’m sure there’s another part to this tune at the very end that sort of brings it back around to the first part.

↳ Posted by Jeremy on March 14th, 2002.

The Sniff of Punch

Yes, Jeremy. After being played in A, it usually goes back to D, but in the higher octave, then there is a bridging part which brings it back to low D, and it starts all over again.

In my experience, this version tends to be frowned ujpon by the more traditional of traditional musicians. I have a strong suspicion it was originally learned from a commercial recording. Can anyone shed any light on this?

There are a number of two- and three- part settings, one of which features in Kevin Burke’s monster 20-tune set on his 1978 album, ‘If the Cap Fits’.

↳ Posted by CreadurMawnOrganig on March 15th, 2002.

Pinch of snuff

I first came across the 9-part version - that’s “low” D - G - A -“high” D and an extra part bringing it back to “low” D - played by Seamus Tansey(flute) and Andrew Davey(fiddle) on the “Music From The Coleman County” LP recorded in1972. I had assumed it was a Sligo version of a reel more commonly associated with Co.Donegal.
The “big” version is not nearly as common these days as it was in the 80s (at least in Scotland), and it’s years since I heard this version played in Ireland.

↳ Posted by Harper_Lad on January 1st, 2004.

Donegal and Sligo

I identified this tune as a piece of sheet music a friend had given me, in a packet of tunes a friend had transcribed from Donegal seisiuns. While Burke and a lot of other people do seem to play the “extended version”, I had to argue with my friend about it. The Donegal sheet music just had it in D: the A and B parts (with a typical recurring Donegal sharp in the B part), then Josh Kane’s “missing part” as the C part. The A part up an octave was listed as an optional variation.

I sent my friend the link to this discussion, so that argument’s settled. Just thought y’all’d be interested in the stylistic discrepancy, in case anyone tries to give you the old “it’s not played that way” line.

In sum: It’s played both ways. Donegal version is 3 parts in D, Sligo goes into all the other keys.

Whew.

Re: The Pinch Of Snuff

Hi Phil,
…it depends what you call the last part.
In your transcription (X:6) the last -descending- part should really be played twice (with a different ending) so as to add up to 8 bars, not 4 bars.
Having said that, each ‘’part‘’ in this reel can be defined as a 16-bar-long ‘tune + turn’ (= 8+8 bars) pair’ so the last, descending, part (in your version) is technically half as long as the said pairs.
As for ‘correctness’ or ‘wrong’, there are no hallowed way of playing tunes like this one, especially when it comes to the number of repeats. You can use the video link above as a guide, although in this ‘version’, the Donegal and Sligo versions are played together, as if they were one extended set of variations.

Re: The Pinch Of Snuff

I did quite a bit of work today on the Pinch of Snuff; it is a tune I heard and learnt early in my trad. music “career” (!) and yet I’ve never held a ‘stabilized’ form for it in my head or fingers, perhaps due to the many versions that have been recorded I have listened to overtime.
There seems to be three main versions:
the ‘Donegal version’ (recorded by the likes of Tommy People or the Glackin brothers), all in D and with the descending bridge in the middle (and/or at the end);
there is the ‘Sligo version’ with up to 9 parts, with the descending part left at the end and going through up to 3 different tonalities (D, G, A and D again).
The version X:2/X:4/X:8 has only two parts.

There are versions (or renditions) that fit within the whistle range (Kevin Burke’s, Cathal McConnel’s) but most make use of the wider fiddle range down to G on the IVth string.

I haven’t yet found versions with 4 parts that would lend meaning to the alternative name ‘The four seasons’ (??)

I sat down and came up with a ‘middle way’ version in 9 parts I am happy to teach if needs be;
I am about to post it here.
It is mostly based on the Crickard brothers / Seamus Creagh & Jacky Daly versions with added higher melodic path tin-whistle options, if you know what I mean.
This endeavour has helped clarify this tune for me. I hope some of youse will find it useful too.

↳ Posted by birlibirdie on June 27th, 2023.

NB:
The bottom C in the 9th/last part is not 1-quaver- but 4-quaver-long (a minim),
unfortunately not all abc programs support this kind of notation:
|GAGE [=c1=C4]eed| but you get the jist (the top line is added to help the beginner whistle, flute or uilleann pipe players)
